items.title: The Geometry of Shadows: What a Bridge Railing Taught Me About the Mathematics of LLMs
items.summary: While running one morning, I found myself staring at the shadows cast by a stone bridge railing. The railing had a series of identical, carved镂空 (hollowed-out) structures. As I ran past, the angle of the sun shifted, and the shadows on the ground transformed. At one moment, the shadow looked like a swimming fish; a few steps later, it looked like a rolling wave; later still, it was just an abstract, elongated blob. It struck me that I was witnessing a perfect physical metaphor for how human language—and Large Language Models (LLMs)—generate meaning. The stone bridge hole is the concept. The sunlight is the context. The shadow on the ground is the utterance. This realization perfectly mirrors the "Central Problem" of language modeling, beautifully stripped of its usual jargon in Joseph L. Breeden’s paper, The Simple Mathematics of Large Language Models . The Problem of the Single Shadow In his paper, Breeden highlights a fundamental flaw in early AI approaches: treating words as static, unchanging symbols. He uses the classic example of the word "bank" : "I deposited money at the **bank ." (a financial institution) "We walked along the river **bank ." (the land beside a river) "The plane **banked * sharply left."* (tilted) If we assign a single, fixed vector to the word "bank" in a high-dimensional space, we are essentially trying to capture all three meanings in one static shape. But as Breeden points out, a fixed vector for "bank" cannot simultaneously be close to "money," "river," and "tilt." In my running metaphor, a single, fixed vector is like looking at the bridge hole only at exactly high noon. You get one specific shadow. But language is dynamic. The meaning of "bank" depends entirely on the "angle of the light" provided by the surrounding words. The Mathematics of Light: Learned Weighted Averaging How does an LLM solve this? Breeden explains that the core mechanism of a Transformer is not magic; it is Learned Weighted Averaging . Let’s map Breeden’s mathematics to the bridge railing: 1. The Bridge Hole (The Token Embedding, $e$) Before any context is applied, the word "bank" is just an initial embedding vector ($e$). It is the physical stone structure itself. It contains the potential for all its meanings, but it is currently unshaped by the environment. 2. The Angle of the Sunlight (Influence Scores, $a_i \cdot b_j$) To determine what the shadow will look like, we need light. In an LLM, the "light" comes from the surrounding words (the context). Breeden explains that the model computes an influence score between the target word and its context. It does this by projecting the vectors through learned matrices ($W^A$ and $W^B$). When the context is "deposited money," the "light" hits the bridge hole from a financial angle. When the context is "river," the light hits it from a geographical angle. The dot product ($a_i \cdot b_j$) measures how perfectly the angle of the light aligns with the shape of the hole. 3. The Shadow on the Ground (Context-Dependent Representation, $h_i$) Finally, the light passes through the hole and casts a shadow. Mathematically, the model takes a weighted average of the context vectors (using the content projection $W^C$), resulting in a brand new vector ($h_i$). This new vector is the shadow. It is a context-dependent representation . The "bank" in the first sentence is mathematically pulled toward the geometry of finance; the "bank" in the second sentence is pulled toward the geometry of nature. They are the same material, but entirely different products. Why This Metaphor Matters What makes Breeden’s explanation so profound is that it removes the anthropomorphic jargon of "Queries," "Keys," and "Values." There is no little homunculus inside the computer "looking up" information in a database. There is only geometry and light. When an LLM reads the sentence "The plane banked sharply left," it doesn't "know" what a plane is. Instead, the high-dimensional vectors for "plane" and "sharply left" act as a specific angle of light. This light passes through the "bank" bridge hole and casts a shadow that aligns perfectly with the geometric region of "physical motion" in the model's latent space. Furthermore, this explains the difference between languages. In English, "bank" is a single, multi-purpose bridge hole that requires complex, dynamic lighting (Attention mechanisms) to cast the right shadow. In Chinese, the language has already carved three separate, distinct bridge holes: 银行 (bank), 岸 (riverbank), and 倾斜 (to tilt). The Chinese model requires less "light manipulation" because the physical structures themselves are already disentangled. Conclusion: Meaning is a Projection As I finished my run, I realized that the bridge railing wasn't just casting shadows; it was performing a physical projection. Large Language Models do not store a dictionary of definitions. They store a high-dimensional geometry of concepts. Meaning is not a static object you can hold in your hand; it is a projection. It is the dynamic, mathematical shadow cast when the light of context passes through the structure of language. And just like the shadows on the pavement, the beauty of language lies not in the stone itself, but in how it changes with the light. References: Breeden, J. L. (2026). The Simple Mathematics of Large Language Models. CRC Working Papers.

items.title: Our validator checked files, not frames — the first external user taught us the difference
items.summary: auto-xhs is an open-source system that lets an AI agent (Muse, Dots, or Grok Bot) run a Xiaohongshu account end to end: research, writing, video production, posting, and replying to comments. It works through the browser like a person would — no unofficial APIs. I open-sourced it on Oct 14. On the same day, a user in Vietnam, axiom3356, ran the pipeline as-is, measured the output videos, and filed issue #1: three reproducible visual flaws that our validator, validate.py, had not caught. Not one of them. The three flaws: At a scene change, the picture goes almost blank for about 2 seconds. Cards in the new scene appear one by one, and before the first one lands, there is nothing on screen. The finished video came out at 585 kb/s. For 1080p that is far too low — edges smear. 2 Mb/s is the floor anyone recommends. Two annotation cards in the same area, entering with different delays, can overlap each other. His root-cause note was the part that stung: the validator checked the file — duration, resolution, word counts, silence gaps — but never looked at a single frame. What we changed, all of it credited to his report: Blank frames are now a check. Every 0.5 seconds we grab a frame, shrink it to a small grayscale image, and ask whether it is nearly one flat color. Two seconds of that in a row raises a warning with the rough position. Only ffmpeg and the Python standard library. Low bitrate is now a check. Below 2000 kb/s the validator warns. Our own weather example, rendered with the old settings, is 844 kb/s — it gets warned too, and that warning is correct. The assembler got a bitrate floor: target 3M, cap 4M. A small trap here: we had -crf 21 and -b:v set together, and in that combination ffmpeg follows crf and the bitrate target is ignored. Dropping crf fixed it. The overlapping cards are NOT a machine check, and I want to be plain about why. A frame is pixels. Pixels cannot tell a full-bleed background (fine) from a card cropped by the frame edge (broken). A check built on that would cry wolf every day. So instead the template rules now say: one delayed entrance per area, and cards sharing an area go into a layout container. Prevention, not detection. Both new checks are warn-only. A warning respects the person running the pipeline; a hard error from a check that can misfire does not. The issue is still open, on purpose. If axiom3356 sends a PR, his gets reviewed first and used first — he found the problems and proposed the checks. If you run it and your videos look wrong in a way the validator misses, that is exactly the report I want. And if you have content that repeats daily — weather, a digest, a ranking — playbooks live in scenarios/ and new ones are welcome. Repo: https://github.com/zr9959/auto-xhs

items.summary_html:
Interactive messaging is one of the most effective ways to increase user engagement and eliminate typing friction on WhatsApp. Rather than forcing users to type out responses like "1", "YES", or "MENU", the official Meta WhatsApp Cloud API supports interactive buttons (quick replies, call-to-action buttons) and scrollable list menus (up to 10 options).

In this tutorial, we will build a production-ready, type-safe interactive message handler in TypeScript that parses incoming interactive payloads and routes them into conversational flows.

Understanding WhatsApp Interactive Payloads

When a recipient taps an interactive button or list item, Meta delivers an inbound webhook payload where the message type is set to "interactive".

Inside the interactive object, you will receive either:

  1. button_reply: Contains the id and title of the clicked quick-reply button.
  2. list_reply: Contains the id, title, and optional description of the chosen list row.
Step 1: Defining TypeScript Interfaces

Let's define the strict typings for incoming interactive webhook events:

export interface WhatsAppInteractiveButtonReply {
  id: string;
  title: string;
}

export interface WhatsAppInteractiveListReply {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  description?: string;
}

export interface WhatsAppInteractiveMessage {
  from: string;
  id: string;
  timestamp: string;
  type: 'interactive';
  interactive: {
    type: 'button_reply' | 'list_reply';
    button_reply?: WhatsAppInteractiveButtonReply;
    list_reply?: WhatsAppInteractiveListReply;
  };
}
Step 2: Sending Interactive Quick-Reply Buttons

Here is how to construct and send an interactive button message using Axios and TypeScript:

import axios from 'axios';

interface ButtonPayload {
  to: string;
  bodyText: string;
  buttons: Array<{ id: string; title: string }>;
}

export async function sendInteractiveButtons({ to, bodyText, buttons }: ButtonPayload) {
  const url = `https://graph.facebook.com/v21.0/${process.env.WHATSAPP_PHONE_NUMBER_ID}/messages`;

  const payload = {
    messaging_product: 'whatsapp',
    recipient_type: 'individual',
    to,
    type: 'interactive',
    interactive: {
      type: 'button',
      body: { text: bodyText },
      action: {
        buttons: buttons.map(btn => ({
          type: 'reply',
          reply: { id: btn.id, title: btn.title }
        }))
      }
    }
  };

  const response = await axios.post(url, payload, {
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.WHATSAPP_CLOUD_API_TOKEN}`,
      'Content-Type': 'application/json'
    }
  });

  return response.data;
}
Step 3: Dispatching to Conversational CRM and AI Handlers

Once the interactive webhook arrives at your server, you should route it based on the action ID:

export async function handleInteractiveReply(msg: WhatsAppInteractiveMessage) {
  const customerPhone = msg.from;
  const replyType = msg.interactive.type;
  const actionId = replyType === 'button_reply' 
    ? msg.interactive.button_reply?.id 
    : msg.interactive.list_reply?.id;

  console.log(`Received action ${actionId} from ${customerPhone}`);

  switch (actionId) {
    case 'ACTION_BOOK_DEMO':
      // Move customer into 'Demo Scheduled' stage in CRM
      break;
    case 'ACTION_TALK_HUMAN':
      // Trigger human agent assignment
      break;
    case 'ACTION_FAQ':
      // Pass inquiry to AI Knowledge Base
      break;
    default:
      console.warn('Unhandled interactive ID:', actionId);
  }
}
Enterprise Production Considerations

Managing raw button schemas, translation dictionaries, and state machines across hundreds of concurrent chats can quickly become complex.

Platforms like AI Soul provide a visual drag-and-drop conversational designer where interactive buttons, list menus, and AI fallbacks can be configured with zero boilerplate code. Incoming selections are automatically reflected inside the Conversational CRM and can trigger automated WhatsApp Drip Campaigns or AI Chatbot Solutions.

Conclusion

items.title: Gym Plan Drafter: an open-weight AI that drafts safe, budget-aware workout plans for trainers
items.summary: What I Built Gym Plan Drafter is a small web app for gym trainers. The trainer enters a client's age, job type, goal, experience, days per week, minutes per session, diet type and food budget. In about 10 seconds the app writes a draft weekly workout plan and simple Indian meal ideas. The trainer checks and edits it before the client sees it. Writing a plan by hand takes time, so many clients end up with the same copied sheet. That sheet fails when the client is a vegetarian on a small budget or has only 30 minutes. Who would pay: gym trainers and small gym owners, because it saves time on every new client. I have not asked my first user about pricing yet, so I can't say what they would pay. Demo !Image description !Image description Live app: https://rahul-gym-plan-drafter.streamlit.app/ Code https://github.com/Rahulgupta-63/gym-plan-drafter How I Built It Model: GPT-OSS 20B ( openai/gpt-oss-20b ), an open-weight model, through the Groq API. App: Python and Streamlit, deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud. The hard part was trust, not the model. My first version gave eggs to a vegetarian client, and quinoa, hummus and almonds on a "low budget" plan. A trainer would stop using a tool like that after one bad plan. So I added two layers: Rules in the prompt: exact number of days, minutes that add up, food that fits the diet and budget, no calorie numbers. A checker in code: every plan is tested against these rules. If it fails, the app sends the exact problems back to the model and tries again, up to 2 more times. If it still fails, the plan is shown with a clear warning. Safety choices: I first thought about asking clients for body photos. I dropped the idea, because it is a privacy risk and a photo cannot reliably tell what a body needs. No calorie targets. Under 14: no plan. Under 18: general fitness only, and the plan must tell the trainer to supervise, keep loads light, and tell a parent or guardian. Tests: 170 automated checks on 10 client profiles. They test my rules and retry logic with a fake model. They do not test the model itself. Honest limits: the model runs on Groq's servers through an API, so client details leave the trainer's computer. Don't enter names or medical details. The plans are drafts, not medical advice. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? The product is the rules and the checker, not one model. Because the model is open-weight, I can swap it and run the same checks again. This is not just theory for me: last week a Llama model I used on Groq became unavailable, and I moved to GPT-OSS by changing one line. I did not test a closed model side by side, so I can't claim mine is better. What I can say is that I am not locked to one company's model or price. Next step (not built yet): run a small open model on the gym's own PC, so a client's health details never leave the gym. My First User A gym trainer I know tried the app. They tested a fat-loss profile: an MCA student at KNIT Sultanpur on a 4-day schedule. They told me the plan was "perfect". That is one friendly person, so I treat it as a start, not proof. What they asked for next: they asked if the app could also explain how to perform each exercise. That is the first feature I will add. It is not built yet. AI Disclosure I used an AI assistant (Claude) to help write the code and draft this post. I tested the app, deployed it, showed it to a real trainer, and edited the post myself. Thanks for reading!

What I Built

Gym Plan Drafter is a small web app for gym trainers. The trainer enters a client's age, job type, goal, experience, days per week, minutes per session, diet type and food budget. In about 10 seconds the app writes a draft weekly workout plan and simple Indian meal ideas. The trainer checks and edits it before the client sees it.

Writing a plan by hand takes time, so many clients end up with the same copied sheet. That sheet fails when the client is a vegetarian on a small budget or has only 30 minutes.

Who would pay: gym trainers and small gym owners, because it saves time on every new client. I have not asked my first user about pricing yet, so I can't say what they would pay.

Demo

!Image description
!Image description
Live app: https://rahul-gym-plan-drafter.streamlit.app/

Code

https://github.com/Rahulgupta-63/gym-plan-drafter

How I Built It
  • Model: GPT-OSS 20B (openai/gpt-oss-20b), an open-weight model, through the Groq API.
  • App: Python and Streamlit, deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud.

The hard part was trust, not the model. My first version gave eggs to a vegetarian client, and quinoa, hummus and almonds on a "low budget" plan. A trainer would stop using a tool like that after one bad plan.

So I added two layers:

  1. Rules in the prompt: exact number of days, minutes that add up, food that fits the diet and budget, no calorie numbers.
  2. A checker in code: every plan is tested against these rules. If it fails, the app sends the exact problems back to the model and tries again, up to 2 more times. If it still fails, the plan is shown with a clear warning.

Safety choices:

  • I first thought about asking clients for body photos. I dropped the idea, because it is a privacy risk and a photo cannot reliably tell what a body needs.
  • No calorie targets.
  • Under 14: no plan.
  • Under 18: general fitness only, and the plan must tell the trainer to supervise, keep loads light, and tell a parent or guardian.

Tests: 170 automated checks on 10 client profiles. They test my rules and retry logic with a fake model. They do not test the model itself.

Honest limits: the model runs on Groq's servers through an API, so client details leave the trainer's computer. Don't enter names or medical details. The plans are drafts, not medical advice.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

The product is the rules and the checker, not one model. Because the model is open-weight, I can swap it and run the same checks again. This is not just theory for me: last week a Llama model I used on Groq became unavailable, and I moved to GPT-OSS by changing one line.

I did not test a closed model side by side, so I can't claim mine is better. What I can say is that I am not locked to one company's model or price.

Next step (not built yet): run a small open model on the gym's own PC, so a client's health details never leave the gym.

My First User

A gym trainer I know tried the app. They tested a fat-loss profile: an MCA student at KNIT Sultanpur on a 4-day schedule. They told me the plan was "perfect".

That is one friendly person, so I treat it as a start, not proof.

What they asked for next: they asked if the app could also explain how to perform each exercise. That is the first feature I will add. It is not built yet.

AI Disclosure

I used an AI assistant (Claude) to help write the code and draft this post. I tested the app, deployed it, showed it to a real trainer, and edited the post myself.

items.title: Why I Want My AI Coding Assistant to Ask Before It Acts
items.summary: Most AI coding tools are built around one promise: speed . Type a prompt, get code, move on. But after a while I noticed the speed was costing me something. The AI would edit files I didn't expect, delete things I still needed, or run a command I hadn't read. I'd spend the next hour undoing work I never approved. The problem with "just do it" AI When an AI agent has full permission to write, delete, and execute, every action is a small act of trust you didn't explicitly give. For a throwaway script that's fine. For a real codebase it's not. The failure mode isn't dramatic. It's quiet: A helper function gets "cleaned up" and something subtle breaks A config file gets rewritten with slightly different values A dependency gets bumped and nothing works the next morning What I actually want I want an assistant that treats my codebase like it belongs to someone else. That means: Ask before writing. Show me the change, let me approve it. Show diffs, not summaries. "I updated the auth logic" tells me nothing. A diff tells me everything. Checkpoint every step. If step 4 was wrong, I want to rewind to step 3 — not start over. Ask before running commands. A shell command is the most powerful thing an agent can do. It should be the most gated. The trade-off is worth it Yes, this is slower per action. But it's dramatically faster per outcome , because I'm not spending my afternoon fixing things I never agreed to. If you're on Windows and want an AI editor that works this way, that's the idea behind Arcwright — it's free to start. But the principle applies to whatever tool you use: the AI should earn your trust one approved change at a time.

items.title: MCP vs API: When You Need Which, With Real Benchmarks
items.summary: I built the same small service as a REST API and as a stateless MCP server and measured latency, throughput, bytes and the tokens a model has to read. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com . MCP vs API is not really a choice between two rival technologies. An API (usually REST) is how software talks to your service: your code calls known endpoints. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is how an AI application discovers and calls tools at runtime, and almost every MCP server sits on top of an API. The real question is who is calling: your code, or a model. I built the same five-operation projects service both ways on one machine, as a REST API and as a stateless MCP server with the official TypeScript SDK, and measured what each costs. I measured latency, throughput, bytes on the wire and, most important for agents, the tokens a model has to read. I also measured the MCP server that runs this site. Every number below comes from those runs. TL;DR: MCP or API, which should I use? Use a REST API when your own code is the caller: web and mobile apps, cron jobs, webhooks, service-to-service calls and fixed agent pipelines you control. Add an MCP server when AI clients you don't control (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code, Copilot) should use your service, or when the model must pick tools at runtime. Most products need both, with the MCP server wrapping the API. REST API MCP server Caller Your code, written ahead of time An AI model inside an MCP client Discovery Docs or an OpenAPI file a developer reads tools/list at runtime Wire format HTTP verbs, paths, status codes JSON-RPC 2.0 over Streamable HTTP or stdio Auth Whatever you choose (keys, OAuth, sessions) OAuth 2.1 profile defined by the spec, or bearer tokens Latency in my test (p50) 76 µs 424 µs (848 µs when it wraps the REST API) Throughput, 1 Node process 66,486 req/s 4,595 req/s What it costs a model Nothing until you write function schemas Every tool definition, as input tokens Testing Deterministic unit and contract tests Protocol tests plus prompt-dependent evals What is the difference between MCP and an API? An API is a contract for programs: fixed endpoints, documented ahead of time, called by code a developer wrote. MCP is a contract for AI applications: a server lists its tools with names, descriptions and JSON Schemas, and a model decides at runtime which one to call. MCP doesn't replace your API. It describes a curated slice of it in a form a model can use. MCP was open-sourced by Anthropic in November 2024. In December 2025 Anthropic donated it to the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation , alongside OpenAI's AGENTS.md. The announcement put the count at "more than 10,000 published MCP servers" and listed Claude, Cursor, Microsoft Copilot, Gemini, VS Code and ChatGPT as adopters. The MCP tools specification is explicit about who is in charge: "Tools in MCP are designed to be model-controlled , meaning that the language model can discover and invoke tools automatically." That one sentence is the whole difference. With an API, a developer decides what to call. With MCP, the model does. Is an MCP server just an API wrapper? Usually, yes, and that's fine. In practice an MCP server is a thin adapter: each tool validates its arguments and then calls your existing service or REST API. What MCP adds is a standard way to list tools, a standard call format, tool annotations (read-only, destructive, idempotent), and an OAuth 2.1 flow every MCP client already understands. It does not add business logic. Here is the same operation exposed both ways, sharing one Zod schema: // store.ts: one schema, used by REST validation, OpenAPI and the MCP inputSchema export const SlugInput = z . object ({ slug : z . string (). describe ( ' Project slug, e.g. project-42 ' ), }) // REST: GET /api/projects/:slug if ( req . method === ' GET ' && slug ) { SlugInput . parse ({ slug }) const p = ops . get ( slug ) return p ? json ( res , 200 , { project : p }) : json ( res , 404 , { error : ' not_found ' }) } // MCP: the same operation as a tool (@modelcontextprotocol/server 2.3.1) server . registerTool ( ' get_project ' , { description : ' Get one project by slug. ' , inputSchema : SlugInput , annotations : { readOnlyHint : true }, }, async ({ slug }) => { const p = ops . get ( slug ) return p ? { content : [{ type : ' text ' , text : JSON . stringify ({ project : p }) }], structuredContent : { project : p } } : { content : [{ type : ' text ' , text : `No project with slug ${ slug } ` }], isError : true } }, ) Notice the error path. REST returns a 404 your code branches on. MCP returns isError: true with a sentence, because the reader is a model that will decide what to try next. How does MCP work compared to REST? REST uses many URLs and HTTP verbs. MCP uses one endpoint and JSON-RPC: every call is a POST /mcp with a method such as tools/list or tools/call . Under the 2026-07-28 spec MCP is stateless, so each request carries its protocol version and client capabilities in _meta , plus Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers. The same lookup, both ways: # REST curl http://127.0.0.1:3201/api/projects/project-42 # MCP (2026-07-28, stateless, JSON response mode) curl http://127.0.0.1:3202/mcp \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \ -H 'MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28' \ -H 'Mcp-Method: tools/call' -H 'Mcp-Name: get_project' \ -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{ "name":"get_project","arguments":{"slug":"project-42"}, "_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28", "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo":{"name":"curl","version":"8"}, "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{}}}}' The REST response was 334 bytes on the wire. The MCP response was 758 bytes, because the result carries the data twice: once as a JSON string in a text block and once as structuredContent . That's by design. The spec says a tool that returns structured content "SHOULD also return the serialized JSON in a TextContent block" for backwards compatibility. How I benchmarked MCP vs REST Service. 1,000 in-memory projects with five operations: list (search and tag filter), get, create, update and delete. Both servers share the same store and the same Zod 4.6.7 schemas, so only the protocol layer differs. REST. Plain node:http with Zod validation, port 3201. MCP, direct. @modelcontextprotocol/server 2.3.1 with createMcpHandler in JSON response mode, a fresh McpServer per request (the SDK's documented stateless pattern), and tools calling the store in-process. MCP, wrapping REST. The same MCP server, but each tool calls the REST API over HTTP with fetch . This is the common real-world setup. Runs. Node.js 24.22.0 on an 8 vCPU Intel Xeon VM with 15 GB RAM, everything on localhost. Latency: 20,000 sequential requests per case after 2,000 warm-up requests, timed with process.hrtime . Throughput: autocannon 8.0.0 for 10 seconds after a 3-second warm-up, with 1 and 50 connections. All responses were 200 with no errors. Tokens. Counted with OpenAI's o200k_base tokenizer (tiktoken), on compact JSON. Other models tokenize differently, so treat these as relative sizes. Localhost removes network time on purpose. On a real network both protocols pay the same round trip, so the gap below is pure protocol and framework overhead. Is MCP slower than a REST API? Yes, per request, by a lot in relative terms and very little in absolute terms. A get_project call took 424 µs at the median over MCP against 76 µs over REST, about 5.6 times slower. At 50 connections one Node process served 66,486 REST requests per second against 4,595 MCP requests per second, about 14 times fewer. When the MCP tool called the REST API instead of the store, the median doubled again to 848 µs. Case ( get_project ) p50 p90 p99 Mean REST GET /api/projects/:slug 76 µs 122 µs 274 µs 95 µs MCP tools/call (direct) 424 µs 709 µs 1,164 µs 500 µs MCP tools/call (wraps REST) 848 µs 1,216 µs 1,878 µs 936 µs Throughput, one Node process 1 connection 50 connections Response size REST get 30,944 req/s 66,486 req/s 334 B MCP get (direct) 3,216 req/s 4,595 req/s 758 B MCP get (wraps REST) 1,622 req/s 3,116 req/s 758 B REST list (10 results) 27,566 req/s 48,022 req/s 1,707 B MCP list (10 results) 2,733 req/s 3,285 req/s 3,700 B Where does the time go? A CPU profile of the MCP server under load showed 16.7% of samples in the SDK's request pipeline, 11.5% in Zod (parsing plus JSON Schema conversion), and most of the 25% in Node internals spent converting Node requests into Web Request objects and back. Building the per-request McpServer itself was cheap: 13.4 µs for five tools. Does that matter? For agents, no. A model turn takes hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, so 0.35 ms of protocol overhead is noise. For a high-traffic API that your own frontend calls thousands of times a second, it matters a lot. That's one more reason not to route your app's own traffic through MCP. How many tokens do MCP tools cost? The real cost of MCP is context, not CPU. Clients usually send every tool definition, with name, description and JSON Schema, to the model as input tokens on each request. My five tools cost 591 tokens as returned by tools/list , and 488 tokens once reshaped into plain function-calling definitions. The MCP server behind this site exposes 21 tools that add up to 5,949 tokens. What the model reads Tokens (o200k_base) 5 tools, raw tools/list result 591 Same 5 tools as function-calling definitions 488 OpenAPI 3.1 document for the same 5 operations (compact) 933 Same OpenAPI document, pretty-printed 1,717 fabwaseem.com MCP server, 21 tools 5,949 Its largest tool, update_post 1,027 Its smallest tool, get_site_info 89 One get_project result: REST body 46 One get_project result: full MCP result envelope 140 Three things stand out. First, an OpenAPI document is a poor thing to paste into a prompt: it describes responses, status codes and servers the model doesn't need, and for the same operations it was 1.6 times the raw tool list and 1.9 times the function definitions. Second, one rich tool can cost more than ten small ones. update_post alone is 17% of my site's tool budget because its schema lists every editable field. Third, results are cheap if the client is sensible: the text block and the structuredContent were 46 tokens each, the same as the REST body. Large catalogs get expensive fast. Anthropic's engineering team described one setup where loading tool definitions up front took 150,000 tokens. Letting the agent load only the definitions it needed through code execution with MCP cut that to 2,000 tokens, "a time and cost saving of 98.7%." Clients are adapting too. In Claude Code , tool search is on by default, so "only tool names and server instructions load at session start." When should I use MCP instead of an API? Use MCP when the caller is an AI client you don't build, or when the model must choose actions at runtime. Use a plain API, called from your own code, when the workflow is known in advance. A rule of thumb: if you could write the sequence of calls as a function today, write the function. If a person would phrase the task differently every time, give a model MCP tools. Scenario Use Why Your web or mobile app's frontend REST API (or server actions ) Fast, cacheable, no model involved Stripe-style webhooks, cron jobs, ETL REST API Deterministic, testable Let users manage your product from Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor MCP server Every MCP client can connect with no custom plugin Your own agent with a fixed set of 3-5 actions Function calling against your API Same tokens as MCP, one less hop Internal tools shared by several agents and IDEs MCP server Write once, every client discovers it Teaching an agent how to use those tools An agent skill on top of MCP or a CLI Instructions load only when needed That last row is why "MCP vs API vs Skills" posts keep trending. They answer different questions. The API is the capability, MCP is how a model reaches it, and a skill is the instruction manual for using it well. How do I add an MCP server to an existing REST API? Wrap the API, don't rewrite it. Keep your REST endpoints as the source of truth, then expose a curated set of tools that call them. Reuse your validation schemas, return errors as sentences, and mark read-only and destructive tools with annotations. Start with read-only tools, then add writes behind a narrower OAuth scope. // MCP tool that wraps an existing REST endpoint const API = process . env . API_URL // e.g. https://api.example.com/api/projects server . registerTool ( ' update_project ' , { description : ' Change fields on a project. Only the fields in patch are updated. ' , inputSchema : UpdateInput , annotations : { idempotentHint : true }, }, async ({ slug , patch }, ctx ) => { const r = await fetch ( ` ${ API } / ${ slug } ` , { method : ' PATCH ' , headers : { ' content-type ' : ' application/json ' , // forward the caller's own token so REST authorization still applies authorization : `Bearer ${ ctx . http ?. authInfo ?. token } ` , }, body : JSON . stringify ( patch ), }) if ( r . status === 404 ) return { content : [{ type : ' text ' , text : `No project with slug ${ slug } ` }], isError : true } const data = await r . json () return { content : [{ type : ' text ' , text : JSON . stringify ( data ) }], structuredContent : data } }, ) Design rules I follow, learned from running an MCP server for this site's content: Expose tasks, not endpoints. One publish_post tool beats making the model chain three PATCH calls. Keep descriptions short and front-loaded. Claude Code reads only part of a long description when it matches tool search, so put the key words first. Use scopes. This site issues per-app tokens with scopes like posts:read and posts:write , so a client with a read-only token can't call write tools. Treat annotations as hints. The spec says clients "MUST consider tool annotations to be untrusted unless they come from trusted servers." Enforce permissions on the server. Keep a human in the loop for destructive tools. The same spec says there "SHOULD always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations." For a full build, see my guide to building an MCP server in Next.js with route handlers and bearer auth. Does MCP replace REST APIs? No. MCP depends on APIs. Your frontend, mobile apps, partners and background jobs still need fast, cacheable, versioned HTTP endpoints, and MCP gives them nothing. What MCP replaces is the per-client plugin: instead of writing a ChatGPT plugin, a Cursor extension and a Claude integration, you write one MCP server and every compliant client can use it. Common mistakes when choosing between MCP and an API Generating one MCP tool per endpoint. A 60-endpoint OpenAPI file becomes 60 tools and thousands of tokens on every request. Curate. Routing your own app's traffic through MCP. In my test that cut single-process throughput about 14-fold for nothing. Pasting OpenAPI specs into prompts. The same operations cost 1.6 to 1.9 times more tokens as compact OpenAPI than as tool definitions. Forgetting the double payload. Text plus structuredContent roughly doubles response bytes. Keep results small and paginated. Trusting annotations for security. readOnlyHint is a hint. Check scopes on the server for every call. Building on session state. Since the 2026-07-28 spec there are no sessions. Pass explicit handles in tool arguments instead; see stateless MCP servers . Related: if you do expose MCP, lock it down: MCP security in 2026 covers the OAuth SDK CVEs and per-tool scopes. Choosing a framework for the REST side? I benchmarked Hono vs Express vs Fastify on Node 24, Node 26 and Bun. Key takeaways An API is for code that knows what to call; MCP is for AI models that discover tools at runtime and decide what to call. Most MCP servers should wrap an existing API, reusing its validation schemas and authorization. In my Node.js 24 test, an MCP tool call took 424 µs at the median against 76 µs for the same REST call, and 848 µs when it wrapped the REST API. One Node process served 66,486 REST requests per second against 4,595 over MCP, so keep your app's own traffic on REST. Tokens are MCP's real cost: 5 tools took 488-591 tokens, and this site's 21-tool MCP server takes 5,949 tokens. The same 5 operations cost 933 tokens as compact OpenAPI, 1.6 to 1.9 times the tool definitions, so don't paste API specs into prompts. Expose a small set of task-level tools, scope them per client, and use agent skills to teach the workflow. FAQ What is the difference between MCP and an API? An API is a contract for programs: fixed endpoints that code written by a developer calls. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a contract for AI applications: a server lists tools with names, descriptions and JSON Schemas, and a model decides at runtime which tool to call. Most MCP servers call an existing API underneath. Is an MCP server just an API wrapper? Usually, yes. A typical MCP server is a thin adapter that validates tool arguments and calls your existing service or REST API. MCP adds standard tool discovery through tools/list, a standard call format, tool annotations such as readOnlyHint, and an OAuth 2.1 flow MCP clients understand. It should not duplicate your business logic. Is MCP slower than REST? Per request, yes. In my test on Node.js 24.22 a tool call over MCP took 424 microseconds at the median against 76 microseconds for the same REST call, and one process served 4,595 MCP requests per second against 66,486 REST requests. For agents this is noise, because a model turn takes hundreds of milliseconds or more. How many tokens do MCP tools use? It depends on the schemas. In my test, five tools cost 591 tokens as returned by tools/list and 488 as plain function definitions, counted with the o200k_base tokenizer. The MCP server behind fabwaseem.com exposes 21 tools totalling 5,949 tokens, and its largest tool, update_post, costs 1,027 tokens by itself. When should I use MCP instead of an API? Use MCP when AI clients you don't build, such as Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or VS Code, need to use your service, or when a model must choose actions at runtime. Use a plain API called from your own code when the sequence of calls is known in advance, for example in frontends, webhooks, cron jobs and data pipelines. Does MCP replace REST APIs? No. MCP depends on APIs. Frontends, mobile apps, partners and background jobs still need fast, cacheable, versioned HTTP endpoints. What MCP replaces is the per-client plugin: instead of building separate integrations for each AI app, you publish one MCP server that every compliant client can discover and call. Should I convert my OpenAPI spec into MCP tools? Use it as a starting point, not a one-to-one mapping. One tool per endpoint inflates the tool list the model reads on every request. In my test the same five operations cost 933 tokens as compact OpenAPI versus 488 to 591 as tool definitions. Curate a small set of task-level tools with short descriptions instead. How do MCP, APIs and agent skills fit together? They answer different questions. The API is the capability your service offers. MCP is how a model discovers and calls that capability from any compatible client. An agent skill, a SKILL.md file, teaches the agent the workflow and rules for using those tools, and it loads into context only when a task needs it. Originally published on fabwaseem.com .

Where does the time go? A CPU profile of the MCP server under load showed 16.7% of samples in the SDK's request pipeline, 11.5% in Zod (parsing plus JSON Schema conversion), and most of the 25% in Node internals spent converting Node requests into Web Request objects and back. Building the per-request McpServer itself was cheap: 13.4 µs for five tools.

Does that matter? For agents, no. A model turn takes hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, so 0.35 ms of protocol overhead is noise. For a high-traffic API that your own frontend calls thousands of times a second, it matters a lot. That's one more reason not to route your app's own traffic through MCP.

How many tokens do MCP tools cost?

The real cost of MCP is context, not CPU. Clients usually send every tool definition, with name, description and JSON Schema, to the model as input tokens on each request. My five tools cost 591 tokens as returned by tools/list, and 488 tokens once reshaped into plain function-calling definitions. The MCP server behind this site exposes 21 tools that add up to 5,949 tokens.

What the model reads Tokens (o200k_base) 5 tools, raw tools/list result 591 Same 5 tools as function-calling definitions 488 OpenAPI 3.1 document for the same 5 operations (compact) 933 Same OpenAPI document, pretty-printed 1,717 fabwaseem.com MCP server, 21 tools 5,949 Its largest tool, update_post 1,027 Its smallest tool, get_site_info 89 One get_project result: REST body 46 One get_project result: full MCP result envelope 140

Three things stand out. First, an OpenAPI document is a poor thing to paste into a prompt: it describes responses, status codes and servers the model doesn't need, and for the same operations it was 1.6 times the raw tool list and 1.9 times the function definitions. Second, one rich tool can cost more than ten small ones. update_post alone is 17% of my site's tool budget because its schema lists every editable field. Third, results are cheap if the client is sensible: the text block and the structuredContent were 46 tokens each, the same as the REST body.

Large catalogs get expensive fast. Anthropic's engineering team described one setup where loading tool definitions up front took 150,000 tokens. Letting the agent load only the definitions it needed through code execution with MCP cut that to 2,000 tokens, "a time and cost saving of 98.7%." Clients are adapting too. In Claude Code, tool search is on by default, so "only tool names and server instructions load at session start."

When should I use MCP instead of an API?

Use MCP when the caller is an AI client you don't build, or when the model must choose actions at runtime. Use a plain API, called from your own code, when the workflow is known in advance. A rule of thumb: if you could write the sequence of calls as a function today, write the function. If a person would phrase the task differently every time, give a model MCP tools.

Scenario Use Why Your web or mobile app's frontend REST API (or server actions) Fast, cacheable, no model involved Stripe-style webhooks, cron jobs, ETL REST API Deterministic, testable Let users manage your product from Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor MCP server Every MCP client can connect with no custom plugin Your own agent with a fixed set of 3-5 actions Function calling against your API Same tokens as MCP, one less hop Internal tools shared by several agents and IDEs MCP server Write once, every client discovers it Teaching an agent how to use those tools An agent skill on top of MCP or a CLI Instructions load only when needed

That last row is why "MCP vs API vs Skills" posts keep trending. They answer different questions. The API is the capability, MCP is how a model reaches it, and a skill is the instruction manual for using it well.

How do I add an MCP server to an existing REST API?

Wrap the API, don't rewrite it. Keep your REST endpoints as the source of truth, then expose a curated set of tools that call them. Reuse your validation schemas, return errors as sentences, and mark read-only and destructive tools with annotations. Start with read-only tools, then add writes behind a narrower OAuth scope.

// MCP tool that wraps an existing REST endpoint
const API = process.env.API_URL // e.g. https://api.example.com/api/projects

server.registerTool(
  'update_project',
  {
    description: 'Change fields on a project. Only the fields in patch are updated.',
    inputSchema: UpdateInput,
    annotations: { idempotentHint: true },
  },
  async ({ slug, patch }, ctx) => {
    const r = await fetch(`${API}/${slug}`, {
      method: 'PATCH',
      headers: {
        'content-type': 'application/json',
        // forward the caller's own token so REST authorization still applies
        authorization: `Bearer ${ctx.http?.authInfo?.token}`,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(patch),
    })
    if (r.status === 404) return { content: [{ type: 'text', text: `No project with slug ${slug}` }], isError: true }
    const data = await r.json()
    return { content: [{ type: 'text', text: JSON.stringify(data) }], structuredContent: data }
  },
)

Design rules I follow, learned from running an MCP server for this site's content:

  • Expose tasks, not endpoints. One publish_post tool beats making the model chain three PATCH calls.
  • Keep descriptions short and front-loaded. Claude Code reads only part of a long description when it matches tool search, so put the key words first.
  • Use scopes. This site issues per-app tokens with scopes like posts:read and posts:write, so a client with a read-only token can't call write tools.
  • Treat annotations as hints. The spec says clients "MUST consider tool annotations to be untrusted unless they come from trusted servers." Enforce permissions on the server.
  • Keep a human in the loop for destructive tools. The same spec says there "SHOULD always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations."

For a full build, see my guide to building an MCP server in Next.js with route handlers and bearer auth.

Does MCP replace REST APIs?

No. MCP depends on APIs. Your frontend, mobile apps, partners and background jobs still need fast, cacheable, versioned HTTP endpoints, and MCP gives them nothing. What MCP replaces is the per-client plugin: instead of writing a ChatGPT plugin, a Cursor extension and a Claude integration, you write one MCP server and every compliant client can use it.

Common mistakes when choosing between MCP and an API
  • Generating one MCP tool per endpoint. A 60-endpoint OpenAPI file becomes 60 tools and thousands of tokens on every request. Curate.
  • Routing your own app's traffic through MCP. In my test that cut single-process throughput about 14-fold for nothing.
  • Pasting OpenAPI specs into prompts. The same operations cost 1.6 to 1.9 times more tokens as compact OpenAPI than as tool definitions.
  • Forgetting the double payload. Text plus structuredContent roughly doubles response bytes. Keep results small and paginated.
  • Trusting annotations for security. readOnlyHint is a hint. Check scopes on the server for every call.
  • Building on session state. Since the 2026-07-28 spec there are no sessions. Pass explicit handles in tool arguments instead; see stateless MCP servers.

Related: if you do expose MCP, lock it down: MCP security in 2026 covers the OAuth SDK CVEs and per-tool scopes. Choosing a framework for the REST side? I benchmarked Hono vs Express vs Fastify on Node 24, Node 26 and Bun.

Key takeaways
  • An API is for code that knows what to call; MCP is for AI models that discover tools at runtime and decide what to call.
  • Most MCP servers should wrap an existing API, reusing its validation schemas and authorization.
  • In my Node.js 24 test, an MCP tool call took 424 µs at the median against 76 µs for the same REST call, and 848 µs when it wrapped the REST API.
  • One Node process served 66,486 REST requests per second against 4,595 over MCP, so keep your app's own traffic on REST.
  • Tokens are MCP's real cost: 5 tools took 488-591 tokens, and this site's 21-tool MCP server takes 5,949 tokens.
  • The same 5 operations cost 933 tokens as compact OpenAPI, 1.6 to 1.9 times the tool definitions, so don't paste API specs into prompts.
  • Expose a small set of task-level tools, scope them per client, and use agent skills to teach the workflow.
FAQ What is the difference between MCP and an API?

An API is a contract for programs: fixed endpoints that code written by a developer calls. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a contract for AI applications: a server lists tools with names, descriptions and JSON Schemas, and a model decides at runtime which tool to call. Most MCP servers call an existing API underneath.

Is an MCP server just an API wrapper?

Usually, yes. A typical MCP server is a thin adapter that validates tool arguments and calls your existing service or REST API. MCP adds standard tool discovery through tools/list, a standard call format, tool annotations such as readOnlyHint, and an OAuth 2.1 flow MCP clients understand. It should not duplicate your business logic.

Is MCP slower than REST?

Per request, yes. In my test on Node.js 24.22 a tool call over MCP took 424 microseconds at the median against 76 microseconds for the same REST call, and one process served 4,595 MCP requests per second against 66,486 REST requests. For agents this is noise, because a model turn takes hundreds of milliseconds or more.

How many tokens do MCP tools use?

It depends on the schemas. In my test, five tools cost 591 tokens as returned by tools/list and 488 as plain function definitions, counted with the o200k_base tokenizer. The MCP server behind fabwaseem.com exposes 21 tools totalling 5,949 tokens, and its largest tool, update_post, costs 1,027 tokens by itself.

When should I use MCP instead of an API?

Use MCP when AI clients you don't build, such as Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or VS Code, need to use your service, or when a model must choose actions at runtime. Use a plain API called from your own code when the sequence of calls is known in advance, for example in frontends, webhooks, cron jobs and data pipelines.

Does MCP replace REST APIs?

No. MCP depends on APIs. Frontends, mobile apps, partners and background jobs still need fast, cacheable, versioned HTTP endpoints. What MCP replaces is the per-client plugin: instead of building separate integrations for each AI app, you publish one MCP server that every compliant client can discover and call.

Should I convert my OpenAPI spec into MCP tools?

Use it as a starting point, not a one-to-one mapping. One tool per endpoint inflates the tool list the model reads on every request. In my test the same five operations cost 933 tokens as compact OpenAPI versus 488 to 591 as tool definitions. Curate a small set of task-level tools with short descriptions instead.

How do MCP, APIs and agent skills fit together?

They answer different questions. The API is the capability your service offers. MCP is how a model discovers and calls that capability from any compatible client. An agent skill, a SKILL.md file, teaches the agent the workflow and rules for using those tools, and it loads into context only when a task needs it.

On October 17, DeepSeek dropped V4.1-Flash — a distilled efficiency update with better reasoning per token, shorter outputs, and lower latency. I want to talk about what this means in practice, with code, because the per-token price only tells a tenth of the story.

The multiplication problem

Agents don't make one API call per task. A support agent makes 20–50 calls per conversation: retrieval, reasoning, tool calls, drafts, checks. At 1,000 conversations/month × 30 calls × 2,000 tokens, you're at 60M tokens/month.

  • GPT-4-class at ~$10–30/M tokens: $600–$1,800/month
  • DeepSeek V4.1-Flash at ~$0.50–$2/M: $30–$120/month

Same agent. 10–20x cheaper.

The swap is two lines

DeepSeek's API is OpenAI-compatible. Python example:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key="your-deepseek-key",  # platform.deepseek.com
    base_url="https://api.deepseek.com"
)

resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek-chat",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Classify this ticket..."}],
    max_tokens=500  # cap it — agentic loops + runaway outputs = cost incident
)

LangChain, LlamaIndex, and n8n all accept custom base URLs the same way.

The pattern that actually works in production

Don't just swap models — route by difficulty:

  1. DeepSeek handles the 85–90%: classification, drafting, retrieval QA, formatting.
  2. Frontier model handles the 10–15%: ambiguous complaints, complex multi-step reasoning, low-confidence flags.
  3. Log tokens per conversation from day one. The surprise is never the model price — it's the call count multiplying silently.
  4. Keep a fallback provider. No API has 100% uptime.

We run exactly this cascade in production. CSAT stayed flat across 4,000+ conversations while inference dropped ~15x. Customers can't tell which model answered. Finance can.

Try it this week

A/B test: route half your agent traffic through DeepSeek for one week. Compare resolution rate, CSAT, and cost per conversation. Your own traffic beats any benchmark.

items.title: UNKNOWN Is Not Zero: Notes on Archives and Honest Infrastructure Research
items.summary: I’m working on UINET (Ukraine Influence Network Tracker) — a personal research project that’s still taking shape. October 2026 · Work in progress · Open to discussion I started working on UINET because I wanted to better understand how websites involved in documented online influence operations might be connected through their historical infrastructure. If two sites used the same server, tracking identifier, certificate, or backend service, could I establish when that overlap existed and what it actually meant? The further I got, the more that question changed. Now I spend as much time thinking about what the evidence cannot tell me as I do about what it can. I’m sharing these notes because I’d like to talk with people who have dealt with similar problems. The repository is private while I’m still working through the methods. I’m not announcing a finished tool, asking anyone to adopt it, or claiming to have identified an operator. An overlap isn’t an answer Two websites sharing an IP address doesn’t necessarily mean they have the same operator. They could use common hosting or a CDN. Two sites sharing an analytics identifier might have copied the same legitimate website’s code. A matching backend hostname can be worth investigating without being evidence of common control. What I’m trying to build is a way to keep the observation, its source, and the interpretation separate. Rather than outputting a confident looking connection, I’d rather have a record that says: Here is what matched, here is when it was observed, here is the archived evidence, and here are the explanations that are still possible. Historical archives make this harder. If a page isn’t available, I can’t conclude that it lacked a tracking tag. Maybe it was never captured. Maybe the index query was incomplete. Maybe the archive returned an error, or a capture exists but can’t be retrieved or inspected. Those are different kinds of uncertainty. The rule I keep coming back to is simple: UNKNOWN is not zero. A failed lookup isn’t proof of absence, and a page I couldn’t examine isn’t a negative inspection. Making interrupted research visible Some of the least glamorous work has also been the most useful. I’m building an append only journal for the collection process so that a request is recorded as started before it is made, raw responses can be checked against hashes, and interrupted attempts don’t disappear on restart. If a process stops halfway through a request, it doesn’t get a free extra try. The attempt remains spent, and the outcome can remain UNKNOWN. Otherwise a collector might quietly retry until it gets a convenient answer, making the final data look cleaner than the process really was. In a Linux Codespace, I tested recovery by deliberately killing child processes with SIGKILL at several storage boundaries, including during a temporary raw response write and during journal recovery. Those offline tests passed. That tells me the specific recovery paths behaved as intended in that environment; it doesn’t establish power-loss durability, perfect evidence custody, or the accuracy of any real world investigation. Most of this project has been managed from my iPhone. Moving those particular tests to a Linux Codespace was a practical reminder that the claim should match the environment actually tested, not the one I wish had worked. Why I’m spending time with old archives I’m planning a limited feasibility study of 83 distinct historical domain names drawn from two public documentary source frames: EU DisinfoLab’s September 2022 Doppelganger investigation and the U.S. Department of Justice’s September 2024 Doppelganger affidavit. The set has 56 mentions in the first frame and 32 in the second, with five names appearing in both. That overlap in reports isn’t independent evidence of operator continuity. I’ve also been learning from VIGINUM’s February 2024 Portal Kombat report. Portal Kombat is separate from the 83 name Doppelganger feasibility set; I’m mentioning it as related research, not mixing its sites into that inventory. For the proposed first pass, I want to ask a modest question: is enough dated archive index metadata available to justify attempting deeper historical analysis? Finding an indexed capture would not yet mean I could retrieve and inspect the original HTML or JavaScript. I have draft coverage thresholds, but they’re not approved or fully justified yet. Two objections have been especially useful. A fixed 1,000 row response cap might label the best archived domains incomplete, while one request per domain might turn a transient archive outage into apparent historical missingness. I’m considering bounded pagination or filtering and a finite, explicitly recorded retry budget. I haven’t adopted those changes or run the live census. If the archive doesn’t provide adequate evidence, reporting that limitation could be the outcome. I don’t want to quietly swap difficult domains for easier ones just to make the results look complete. A disagreement I’m glad I didn’t erase An earlier AI assisted adversarial review produced agreement with the classifier on six of eight primary synthetic cases. Two disagreements made me rethink how the rules were written. The examples below are fictional illustrations, not observations about real websites. Imagine two impersonation sites, harbor copy.test and valley copy.test, whose archived pages on October 12, 2023 both include a tag shaped like GTM EXAMPLE1. Now imagine the genuine outlet’s archived page from October 11, 2023 contains that same tag. I might initially see a shared tracking identifier between the two impersonation sites, but the genuine page gives me a plausible copied code explanation. If that is the only shared artifact, what positive evidence remains for common control? For me, the right move is to exclude that tag as operator evidence not to invent another connection because the sites look suspicious. The other disagreement involved a shared backend hostname and incomplete coverage of legitimate reference sites. I’m leaning toward a firmer rule here: missing reference evidence can limit confidence, but it cannot make a weak signal stronger. If I haven’t checked the necessary historical pages, I can’t treat their silence as proof that the backend was unique to the suspicious sites. A later discussion of those cases involved me and AI assistance and was not blind or independent re-adjudication. The original 6/8 result stays in the record. I’m much more interested in getting the rule clear than in retroactively turning a disagreement into a pass. What I’d like to hear from others I’m still thinking about how people handle the boundary between what wasn’t found and what couldn’t be checked. For those who work with archived web data: how do you design a coverage measure that doesn’t punish well archived sites when query limits are hit? What retry budget feels reproducible without being unfriendly to public archives? And when you’ve seen genuine site code copied onto a lookalike, what evidence would persuade you that a remaining technical overlap is meaningful? I’d also be interested in how small research projects preserve collection logs and hashes without overstating what a timestamp or a chain of hashes proves. I don’t yet know whether the historical material will support the question I started with. If it doesn’t, that’s worth understanding too. I’m working on the methods, finding the weak spots, and sharing them because the discussion may be more useful than pretending I’ve already solved them. ──────── Public background reading • EU DisinfoLab (September 27, 2022): Doppelganger — Media clones serving Russian propaganda • U.S. Department of Justice (September 4, 2024): Affidavit in support of seizure warrant, Case 2:24-mj-01395 (PDF) • VIGINUM / SGDSN (February 12, 2024): Portal Kombat — A structured and coordinated pro-Russian propaganda network These sources document the context for my research. They are not independent validation of UINET or its current classification results. No live historical domain census has been run for this progress note.

items.title: Why parsing real estate contracts with LLMs is ten times harder than tutorials claim
items.summary: When we started building the data pipeline for NovAsia (a property catalog and market tool for Southeast Asia), the plan looked embarrassingly simple on paper: Grab property PDFs and developer contracts (SPAs). Run them through a modern vision LLM. Dump structured JSON into PostgreSQL. Call it a day. Two weeks in, the pipeline was completely broken. Here is why standard tutorial advice fell apart in production, and what we had to change to get reliable data out of scanned documents. The stuff tutorials don't warn you about Most LLM document parsing demos use crisp, born-digital PDFs with clean typography. In emerging markets like Cambodia and Thailand, reality looks very different: Phone scans: Half the documents are multi-generation scans or photos taken with a phone camera under uneven lighting. Dual-language layout: Khmer or Thai text mixed with English, often in adjacent table columns where line baselines don't match. Physical stamps: Red rubber stamps, signatures, and notary seals placed directly over critical numbers (payment milestone dates, sinking fund fees, transfer taxes). The 40-page prompt trap: If you shove a 35-page PDF into a long-context model and ask for "all fees and payment dates", it will extract 80% correctly and quietly hallucinate the rest with total confidence. When we started building the data pipeline for NovAsia (a property catalog and market tool for Southeast Asia), the plan looked embarrassingly simple on paper:

Grab property PDFs and developer contracts (SPAs).

Run them through a modern vision LLM.

Dump structured JSON into PostgreSQL.

Call it a day.

Two weeks in, the pipeline was completely broken. Here is why standard tutorial advice fell apart in production, and what we had to change to get reliable data out of scanned documents.

The stuff tutorials don't warn you about
Most LLM document parsing demos use crisp, born-digital PDFs with clean typography. In emerging markets like Cambodia and Thailand, reality looks very different:

Phone scans: Half the documents are multi-generation scans or photos taken with a phone camera under uneven lighting.

Dual-language layout: Khmer or Thai text mixed with English, often in adjacent table columns where line baselines don't match.

Physical stamps: Red rubber stamps, signatures, and notary seals placed directly over critical numbers (payment milestone dates, sinking fund fees, transfer taxes).

The 40-page prompt trap: If you shove a 35-page PDF into a long-context model and ask for "all fees and payment dates", it will extract 80% correctly and quietly hallucinate the rest with total confidence.

Three practical changes that fixed it
Instead of trying to find one magic model that does everything, we broke the pipeline down into smaller, boring steps:

  1. Aggressive image cleanup before text extraction

Before any model sees the page, we run basic OpenCV passes: deskewing, binarization, and contrast normalization. Removing phone-scan shadows did more for extraction accuracy than upgrading to a larger model tier.

  1. Section-level chunking with rigid schema validation

We stopped asking the model to parse whole documents at once. We chunk by specific section (e.g., "Schedule of Payments", "Maintenance Obligations") and enforce strict Pydantic schemas. If a field fails validation or falls outside expected bounds, the pipeline flags it for manual check rather than guessing.

  1. Treating tables and narrative text as separate problems

Vision models are great at answering qualitative questions ("under what conditions is the deposit refundable?"), but notoriously sloppy with columns in financial tables. We split table extraction into dedicated passes with explicit row-by-row checks.

The takeaway
If you're building with LLMs on messy, physical-world paperwork, raw context window size won't save you. Most of the reliability comes from image hygiene and strict schema boundaries.

Happy to trade notes if anyone else here is wrestling with noisy scans and table extraction.

items.title: Giving AI a “crystal clear” view of the materials world
items.summary: In principle, artificial intelligence could make finding the right material for an application as simple as ordering dinner: Scientists would tell a large language model what they want, and it would serve them a perfectly designed crystal for the job. Unfortunately, that approach doesn’t work well yet, and the problem comes down to data: Most materials consist of crystals, which are 3D periodic arrangements of atoms whose structures are stored in specialized formats, not the text streams that today’s large language models are trained on. The experimental literature is also heavily biased toward a few popular classes of crystals, making AI outputs skew toward those materials. Now MIT researchers have created a multimodal AI model that tackles these problems. The model combines 3D atomic structures with natural language descriptions to create rich linguistic descriptions about the structures from experimental research papers and first-principles computational databases. The unified description outlines not just the chemical composition and structure, but also its properties, processing considerations, and potential applications, helping AI learn more about what makes materials impactful. In a new paper in Nature Communications , the researchers showed their system could identify better material designs than models trained on text streams alone by allowing the model to “see” the atomic arrangements and bonding patterns. For example, when the researchers asked the model to identify materials suited for solid-state lithium-ion battery electrolytes, its top results included materials that had been independently identified as promising candidates. The researchers also showed their model learned geometric representations of material structures in ways text-only models could not. “Structure is really at the heart of the materials science field,” says Ju Li, the Carl Richard Soderberg Professor in Power Engineering in the Department of Materials Science and Engineering (DMSE). “If you understand the structure, you can infer quite a lot about the properties and performance of materials. We wanted to build the connection between a material’s atomic structure and its properties and processing for the model.” Joining Li on a paper about the model are Yang Jeong Park, first author and former MIT postdoc; Mayank Kumaran, a recent University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign computer engineering graduate; Chia-Wei Hsu SM ’26; and Elsa Olivetti, the Jerry McAfee (1940) Professor in Engineering in DMSE. Getting models to see in 3D Materials scientists are always on the hunt for new crystals that will lead to the products of the future. Over the last decade, AI has reshaped that process, proposing and designing new crystalline structures, which have highly ordered atomic structures and make up more than 90 percent of solid materials on Earth. Most of those models treat solid crystalline materials as 3D graphs. The rise of large language models has given researchers another tool for innovation. But existing large language models rely heavily on text from published papers and books, limiting their knowledge of the physical world, since many potential crystal structures are stored in computational databases. Text-based models also lack understanding of visual geometry. To overcome those challenges, the researchers decided to create a vision-language model for crystalline materials. They trained a language model to create textual descriptions of crystal structures using an approach known as contrastive learning, in which models compare similar and dissimilar examples of structures and textual descriptions to achieve a unified understanding. This is similar to aligning the visual and language regions of the brain. Following training, the researchers compared the predictions of two versions of the model: one trained on a dataset containing the AI-generated descriptions and the other trained on a dataset containing text from papers only. They found that the model trained on AI-generated descriptions successfully learned how to align geometric structures with text descriptions while the other did not. “We wanted to create an AI model that works broadly across materials,” Li says. “That’s why we decided to synthesize narratives rather than rely solely on existing papers. We found when we used that narrative dataset, the models are better at predicting the function.” Accelerating materials science The researchers then showed their model could be given a natural language query describing a property and identify crystalline materials with that property, outperforming a baseline. “There are sometimes these step changes within materials science around algorithmic integration toward useful tools, which the community uses to further advance the field,” Olivetti says. “This approach helps us see more deeply into three-dimensional structures and link structures to property and processing. I hope this can be one of those step changes.” Li compares the model to AlphaFold, an AI model that links protein structures with function that has helped advance biological research and drug development. The researchers believe their new approach can work with many crystalline materials, and they hope other material scientists will use it to accelerate their work. “Being able to see a three-dimensional crystal and how its atoms are connected is super foundational,” Li says. “I think this will be useful to anyone who practices materials science.” The work was supported, in part, by the U.S. Defense Threat Reduction Agency through the University Research Alliance; the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency; and the National Research Foundation of Korea.
